slides.title: Meet the jellyfish
slides.newHtml:
Meet the jellyfish

Over 2,000 species worldwide — around for >600 million years
Simple animals — yet thriving in Earth’s oceans
  • No brain, heart, blood or bones — around 95% water
  • Stinging tentacles catch small fish (and even other jellyfish)
  • Nerve net coordinates responses; some glow in the dark
  • Numbers are increasing in warmer, more acidic oceans

slides.title: Exam question: are jellyfish alive? [3]
slides.oldHtml:
Exam question: are jellyfish alive? [3]

Jellyfish swim by rhythmic pulsations of the umbrella … usually feed on small fish … take oxygen into their cells directly from the water … have a nerve net which can coordinate responses … release sperm or eggs into the water.
Give 3 pieces of evidence that jellyfish are living.
swim → movement · feed → nutrition · sperm and eggs → reproduction · oxygen → respiration · nerve net → control
slides.newHtml:
Exam question: are jellyfish alive? [3]

Read the passage

Jellyfish swim by pulsing their umbrella-shaped bell and feed on small fish caught in their stinging tentacles.

They absorb oxygen directly from the water and have a nerve net that coordinates responses.

Most jellyfish release sperm or eggs directly into the water.

Suggest and explain 3 pieces of evidence that jellyfish are living.
  • Swim → movement
  • Feed on small fish → nutrition
  • Take in oxygen → respiration
  • Nerve net coordinates responses → sensitivity / control
  • Release sperm and eggs → reproduction

slides.title: Pathogens and diseases
slides.newHtml:
Pathogens and diseases

Fungi
  • Trichophyton → athlete’s foot
  • Candida → thrush
  • Diplocarpon → rose black spot
Bacteria
  • ★ Pneumococcus → pneumonia
  • Vibrio cholerae → cholera
  • Salmonella → food poisoning
  • Mycobacterium → TB
Protoctists
  • ★ Plasmodium → malaria
  • Entamoeba → amoebic dysentery
  • Phytophthora → potato blight
Viruses (not a kingdom)
  • ★ Influenza → flu, ★ HIV → AIDS
  • ★ Tobacco mosaic virus → leaf mottling
  • Measles virus → measles
★ Named in the Edexcel IGCSE specification, Animals and plants are not microbial pathogens (though mosquitoes act as vectors).

slides.title: Food tests: lab tips
slides.newHtml:
Food tests: lab tips

PREP FIRST: Crush solid foods with ~5–10 mL water (let bits settle or filter) — use only ~2 mL per tube — avoid dark foods (e.g. beetroot, soy sauce) that hide colours — keep glassware clean
Starch — Iodine
  • Use a white spotting tile so blue-black stands out
  • Only 2–3 drops of iodine on a tiny piece or drop — instant
  • Best foods: potato, bread, rice, pasta (not sugar!)
Glucose — Benedict’s
  • Equal volumes: ~2 mL food + ~2 mL Benedict’s
  • Heat in a ~80 °C water bath for 5 min (no direct Bunsen)
  • Best foods: apple juice, honey, onion (not table sucrose!)
Protein — Biuret
  • Add ~2 mL biuret to ~2 mL sample, shake gently (no heat)
  • Hold against white paper — weak positives are pale lilac
  • Best foods: egg white, milk, tofu, grated cheese
Lipids — Emulsion
  • Ethanol first (~2 mL) + tiny smear, shake hard to dissolve fat
  • Then pour into ~2 mL cold water (keep ethanol off flames!)
  • Best foods: cooking oil, butter, crushed nut or sunflower seed
🧪 Teacher prep: making Biuret from CuSO₄(aq) + NaOH(aq)
Best bench method: 2 separate bottles (no precipitate!)
  • Biuret A (alkali): 5–10% NaOH(aq) (~1–2 M; or 0.4 M / 16 g/L for lower-hazard KS4)
  • Biuret B (dilute copper sulfate): 0.5–1% CuSO₄(aq) (5–10 g CuSO₄·5H₂O per L — pale sky-blue; or dilute 1 M stock 1 : 25 with water)
  • Class steps: Add ~2 mL NaOH(aq) to ~2 mL sample, swirl, then add 3–5 drops CuSO₄(aq) & shake gently → lilac/purple
⚠ Don’t mix plain CuSO₄ + NaOH in one bottle!
Plain Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ immediately precipitates insoluble blue Cu(OH)₂(s). To pre-mix 1 L in one bottle you need a chelator: dissolve 1.5 g CuSO₄·5H₂O + 6 g Rochelle salt (Na K tartrate) in 500 mL water, stir in 300 mL 10% NaOH, top up to 1 L.
Safety & pro tips
Goggles mandatory (NaOH is corrosive) · keep CuSO₄ very pale blue (too dark masks faint lilac) · best control = 1 part egg white : 4 parts water (swirl gently, don’t froth).

Sharing electrons can build either tiny separate molecules or one giant network

A giant 3D tetrahedral network of carbon atoms
  • Each carbon forms 4 strong covalent bonds to 4 other carbons
  • Extremely hard — rigid 3D lattice in every direction
  • Very high melting point (above 3550 °C) — lots of energy needed to break strong bonds
  • Does not conduct electricity — no delocalised electrons

Flat hexagonal layers of carbon atoms
  • Each carbon forms 3 strong covalent bonds (leaving 1 free electron per atom)
  • Soft & slippery — only weak forces between layers, so sheets slide over one another
  • Conducts electricity — delocalised electrons move freely along layers
  • Very high melting point (~3650 °C) — strong bonds within each sheet
  • Uses: pencil lead, solid lubricants, electrodes

slides.title: Worked example: Mercury
slides.newHtml:
Worked example: Mercury

QUESTION: Mercury takes 87.97 days to orbit the Sun. Orbital radius = 57.91 million km. Find its orbital speed.
Step 1 — One orbit distance (2πr)
2 × π × 57.91 million km = 363.9 million km
Step 2 — Divide by time period (T)
363.9 million ÷ 87.97 = 4.14 million km/day
Step 3 — Convert to m/s (1 day = 86 400 s)
4 140 000 000 m ÷ 86 400 s = 47 900 m/s

Main sequence stars

For most of a star’s life, it is stable:
Inward force
Gravity pulls all the gas inwards
Outward force
Heat & radiation pressure from hydrogen fusion push outwards
Inward gravity = Outward pressure → STABLE

  • The outer layers expand enormously
  • Its surface becomes much cooler
  • Cooler surface → glows red
Later it sheds its outer layers, leaving a tiny, hot white dwarf
